source.title_on_document: CreAItive Collaboration? Users' Misjudgment of AI-Creativity Affects Their Collaborative Performance

supplement.where: Referred to as 'Supplementary Materials'; the document gives no URL or location.
supplement.holds: Detailed description of the AUT scoring, informed consent form, task interface screenshots, all questionnaires, detailed descriptive statistics of the sample and the group-difference (bias) analyses, and two exemplary human-AI interactions. The main text prints no standard deviations for most AUT outcomes; whether the supplement holds them is not stated.

paper_design_summary: Second-semester Computer Science students at an Austrian university worked in pairs (52 dyads, 104 people). On arrival, dyads were randomly assigned to do three Alternate Uses Test (AUT) items with off-the-shelf ChatGPT-4 available in a chat window (copy-paste disabled) or without AI. All dyads then did one more AUT item without AI (immediate post-test), and three weeks later each participant did three AUT items alone and online without AI (retention post-test); outputs were scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration.

studies.label: Dyad AUT experiment: ChatGPT-4 vs no AI, with unaided immediate and three-week retention post-tests

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to off-the-shelf ChatGPT-4 in a chat window during the three main-test AUT items (experimental AI group) versus no AI (control non-AI group)
assignment.quote: Upon arriving at the study location, dyads were randomly assigned to their experimental condition.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 4, Section 3: 'This study was also preregistered on AsPredicted (https://aspredicted.org/msym-tbc2.pdf)'; hypotheses H1-H3 on flexibility and originality; p. 11-12, Section 6.4

arms.name: Experimental AI group
arms.description: Dyads with off-the-shelf ChatGPT-4 in a chat window inside the task interface during the three main-test AUT items; copying and pasting AI answers into the submission window was disabled. No AI in the immediate or retention post-tests.

arms.name: Control non-AI group
arms.description: Dyads doing the same three main-test AUT items without AI; no AI in the post-tests.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports only the valid sample (52 dyads/104 participants, 26 dyads/52 participants per condition). It says that only native or advanced German-speaking dyads were included in the final sample (participation was offered in English and German), but gives no number of dyads randomized or excluded. Figure 1 shows 52 vs 52 participants in the retention post-test; no attrition is reported.
participants.who: Students from a 2nd-semester Computer Science introductory lecture on data science and AI; ages 18-35, mean 21.55; 77.88% male; 99.04% had used generative AI before; 5% course bonus for participation
participants.quote: The valid sample consisted of 52 dyads/104 participants, with 26 dyads/52 participants per experimental condition.
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 4.3 Sample; p. 5, Section 4.2.1 and Figure 1

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (off-the-shelf, no prompt engineering by the research team; reference [80]: gpt-4, version March 2024)
ai_tool.how_used: Chat window in the AUT interface; dyads prompted freely (user-led) and typed any AI-generated uses they wanted into the submission window, since copy-paste was disabled. About half of entered answers were AI-generated (7.60 of 15.22 on average, Table 5).

task.description: Alternate Uses Test done collaboratively by dyads sharing one display: main test objects fork, flower pot, suitcase; immediate post-test object glass bottle (both conditions without AI); retention post-test done individually online, objects key, brick, gymnastics ball.
task.duration: Four minutes per AUT item; the on-campus session (main test plus immediate post-test) lasted approximately one hour; retention post-test three weeks after the main test.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned dyads to ChatGPT-4 access or no AI on the AUT (p. 5, Section 4.2.2); 104 people analyzed in 52 dyads, 52 per arm (p. 6, Section 4.3), so the 50-person rule holds even counting dyads; outcomes are AUT fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration scored on the dyads' answers. Assignment is clustered by dyad. S2 (pre-study) is AI vs human context only.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT-4, dyads did not score higher on AUT fluency (14.6 vs 12.7), originality (3.7 vs 3.7), or flexibility (10.0 vs 9.4) but scored lower on elaboration (2.1 vs 3.8; U = 924.0, p = 0.005), the elaboration gap persisted in the unaided immediate post-test (2.8 vs 4.7; U = 970.0, p = 0.012), and no differences remained three weeks later (pp. 7-9, Figures 4, 8, 12).
open_questions: Unit of the Mann-Whitney tests is unclear: with 26 vs 26 dyads the maximum U is 676, yet the paper prints U = 924.0 (main-test elaboration) and U = 970.0 (immediate post-test elaboration). The tests may use participant-level (52 vs 52) or item-level rows. The sample-balance tests (U = 1038.5, U = 1631.0) are at participant level.

Figure 12 (retention post-test, done individually) has the header 'nAI = 26 dyads, nCONTROL = 26 dyads', while Figure 1 shows 52 vs 52 participants; the retention sample size is not stated in the text.
Number of dyads randomized and how many were dropped by the German-language restriction are not stated.
Who coded elaboration (and the originality categories) is not stated in the main text; scoring details are in the Supplementary Materials, which are not in this PDF.
Figure 11 (immediate post-test elaboration) is titled 'Main Test: Elaboration Distribution' inside the chart, but its caption says immediate post-test.
notes: Preregistered hypotheses (H1-H3) concern flexibility and originality, so those are marked preregistered_primary; fluency and elaboration are marked secondary. The paper reports no overall creativity score and no diversity-across-people outcome. Outcomes are mean indices over three AUT items per dyad for the main test, one item for the immediate post-test, and three individual items for the retention post-test. Except immediate post-test fluency (means and SDs in text), arm levels come only from bar labels in Figures 4, 8, and 12; no SDs, standard errors, or test statistics are printed for the nonsignificant outcomes. Also reported but not coded: a Spearman correlation between the AI-answer acceptance rate and main-test fluency in the AI group (rho_s = 0.424, p = 0.002, p. 10, Figure 14), prompt specificity, and perception questionnaires. Age and private AI use differed between arms (p. 6).
